confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 14 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Marchese, Lynell. 1986. Tense/aspect and the development of auxiliaries in Kru languages. SIL Publications in Linguistics 78. Dallas: Summer Institute of Linguistics and University of Texas at Arlington.
catalog_locator: Marchese 1986: sec. 1.4.1 p. 16; ch. 2 p. 54; ch. 5 (Exbraciation) p. 261 (printed pages; scanned and read).
catalog_quote: Kru has both lexical and grammatical tone. Languages have either three or four register tones ... Tone plays an extremely important role in the grammatical systems of the Kru family, making such distinctions as perfective/imperfective aspect, possessive/relative/subject pronouns, definite/indefinite, and sometimes singular/plural. ... [p. 54] in examining the Dewoin verbal system, we note that there is a set of pronouns which Welmers (1977b) describes as "presumptive." These pronouns, characterized by a lengthened low-tone vowel, are used to designate future and customary actions. ... [p. 261] there has been no systematic study of stress in the Kru group as a whole

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Marchese 1986, printed p. 261 (p. 275; the page scan), §5.6.2, comparing the Neo-Melanesian future particle 'bai' with Kru tense markers: "Second, the Neo-Melanesian particle bai loses stress. While there has been no systematic study of stress in the Kru group as a whole (an exception to this is Innes's (1966) and Luckau's (1975) studies of Grebo stress where it is claimed that stress in Grebo is contrastive), there is a parallel between loss of stress in Neo-Melanesian and the shift from independent word to verbal suffix in Kru." This is a statement about Kru generally and about Grebo (contrastive stress per Innes 1966, Luckau 1975), not about Dewoin; it gives no placement rule and does no…

new_statements.quote: In Krahn and Guere, parts of "le conglomerat krahn-guere-wobe", and in the related languages Bassa and Dewoin, links have been noted between consonant type and tone (see Tisher [1979] for Krahn, B&L for Guere, Hobley [1964] for Bassa, and Welmers [1975] for Dewoin). In general, the consonant inventories can be divided into voiceless, voiced, and implosive. [...] Though there are exceptions, the usual pattern is that a voiced consonant in these languages lowers the onset of the following tone.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Dewoin has lexical tone whose realisation interacts with onset consonant type: (non-implosive) voiced consonants lower the onset of the following tone (depressor effect), per Welmers's 1975 field notes as reported by Singler; no tone inventory and nothing on stress is given.
new_statements.exceptions: 'Though there are exceptions' (unspecified) to the voiced-consonant lowering pattern; in Wobe the pattern no longer holds.
new_statements.identity_note: Article is about Wobe (Wè Northern, wobe1242); the quoted remark names 'Bassa and Dewoin' as related Western Kru languages of Liberia and cites Welmers's 1975 UCLA Dewoin field notes — unambiguously dewo1238. The statement is second-hand (Singler reporting Welmers ms). | Same work as A's index 7 (A marked it silent). Dewoin = the Western Kru language of Liberia, data from Welmers 1977 (exx. 31-32 are Dewoin, tone-marked); the sentence names Dewoin explicitly alongside Klao, Grebo, Krahn, Wobé, Nyabwa — dewo1238. | group-level statement; Dewoin is named on p.2 ('several isolates: Kuwaa and Dewoin in Liberia (confirmed)') and in the noun-class agreement table p.9; the tone remark is about the Kru family as a whole [name in source: Dewoin; pages 1-2, 4, 9]

sources.note: The only De/Dewoi content is a one-paragraph ethnographic note ('Les De ou Do (appelés aussi Dewoi) habitent entre Monrovia et le fleuve Lofa..', pp. 71-72) and the De numerals, which Delafosse states he took from Koelle ('la numération de à Koelle', p. 72); the bibliography lists 'Dé. — Koelle : vocabulaire dewoi.' Nothing on De phonology or stress. In the general preface (p. 3) Delafosse says alphabetic signs cannot show 'l'accent tonique ou plutôt l'intonation' and he only marks it in special notes; none such for De. Glottolog's 'grammar sketch' label is misleading for this language.
